units.text: One person may correctly calculate an object’s orbit without intuitively imagining it in every detail. Another may draw a highly convincing but incorrect picture. Which one understands? The question shows that we use the same word for different competencies.

We can recognize a pattern, predict, explain a mechanism, identify what would change if we intervened and connect the result to a more general structure. These capacities sometimes support one another but do not coincide. A results table can predict without explaining. A causal story can seem clear and fail numerically.

Understanding also has an aspect of transfer. If I memorize an answer for one situation without knowing when it applies, my competence is fragile. If I can systematically modify conditions and anticipate which part of the answer remains, I have grasped something deeper. A well-understood law is not merely a correctly reproduced formula, but a map of dependencies and limits.

Mathematics extends this ability because it allows precise tracking of relationships, including when visual intuition gives way. But it does not eliminate the representation problem. We must decide which quantities correspond to the world, what we ignore and which measurements can check the result. An impeccable calculation may answer an unsuitable question.

Why does the world seem so accessible to mathematical descriptions? We can consider their success evidence of its structure. We can also notice selection: we call precisely the descriptions that worked ‘discovered laws’, while failed attempts disappear from textbooks. The two observations do not cancel each other. Selection explains part of our retrospective picture without making the existence of exploitable regularities trivial.

Nor is there a simple reason why an evolved brain had to understand the entire universe. For many biological functions, distinguishing opportunities and dangers at the scale of its life would suffice. Microscopic or cosmological understanding is achieved through cultural extensions: languages, instruments, mathematics, institutions of verification. This observation about supports’ role establishes no fixed limit to mind; it shows that ‘what humans can do’ is not reducible to an unaided individual’s intuition.

Relativity offers a historical example: understanding required revising assumptions about simultaneity, clocks and geometry, not merely more precise measurements in the old vocabulary. In his exposition for the public, Einstein connects concepts to measurement procedures and shows why time cannot simply be treated as an identical background for every observer. In general relativity, spacetime geometry participates in describing gravity. These conceptual changes do not mean nature changed its rules when physicists changed the theory (Einstein, 1916/1920) .

Our ability to learn such a framework matters for the question of mental limits. An intuition formed in everyday circumstances is not an infallible judge of physical possibility. But not every counterintuitive idea deserves adoption either. The gain comes from testable relationships enabled by the new framework, not its difficulty or distance from common sense.

Artificial intelligence makes the difference between finding a relationship and human understanding of it more visible. The AI Feynman system uses symbolic regression and physics-inspired heuristics to recover formulas from data, evaluated partly on a set of known equations. The results show the power of guided-search methods; they do not demonstrate automatic discovery of the universe’s foundations (Udrescu și Tegmark, 2020) .

SINDy seeks dynamical descriptions with few nonzero terms chosen from a candidate library. It makes a fruitful assumption explicit: dynamics may be simple in suitable coordinates and bases. Success nevertheless depends on representation, data and the list of possibilities supplied to the method. Finding the equation in a chosen vocabulary is not identical to inventing the relevant vocabulary (Brunton, Proctor și Kutz, 2016) .

Now imagine an AI predicting an experiment better than humans but producing a model nobody can explain in one page. There are at least three options. We can reject the model because it does not resemble our understanding. We can trust it without limit because it predicts well. Or we can separate use from justification: test it outside its construction data, investigate stability and seek partial explanations of important mechanisms.

The third option is most promising. It does not demand that every truth fit our working memory, but neither does it transfer authority to an opaque box. We can understand conditions under which a result is reliable even without holding every operation that produced it in mind. At the same time, for risky interventions, prediction without knowledge of limits may be insufficient.

Can there be a true law the human mind cannot understand? It depends on ‘understand’. Perhaps we cannot visualize it. Perhaps we cannot compute its consequences unaided. Perhaps we cannot formulate suitable concepts. These difficulties do not prove a definitive cognitive frontier exists. But past success does not guarantee that every structure of the world will become transparent to us either.

The most productive question is more concrete: what extension would let us understand the next relationship? A notation, a new experiment, a simulation, a verification tool or a collective concept? Sometimes the mind does not overcome a limit through greater effort in the same form. It changes its way of working.
